1.0 Introduction
e
35
36
Wellbeing has emerged as an influential agenda in the built w environment in recent years1,
37
promoting the social and, significantly, the economic aspects of triple bottom line
38
39 sustainability. It embodies an accessible and affirmative goal for occupants and practitioners
40 alike, compared to the technical discourse of restraint that surrounds energy efficiency. Its
41 growing prominence is reflected in the emergence of new valuation practices in the built
42 environment, particularly around the “business case” for wellbeing and a range of associated
43 metrics and frameworks for this end2 3 4. Interestingly, increased wellbeing is often
44
associated with anticipated improvements in occupant performance, particularly productivity2,
45
yet the existing frameworks for evaluation do not explicitly prove this relationship, nor
46
47 generate learning about how it can be achieved in practice. As the property market
48 increasingly demands user-centred environments, evidence-based design proven to deliver
49 wellbeing outcomes for end users is essential. The challenge of capturing and disseminating
50 this evidence to a range of expert and non-expert audiences is therefore a topical
51
professional concern, and requires an evaluative shift away from measuring building
52
performance towards measuring the outcomes experienced by people5.
53
54
55 2.0 Wellbeing in the built environment
56
57
58
Page 1 of 16
59
60 http://mc.manuscriptcentral.com/bsert

Page 3 of 33 Building Services Engineering Research and Technology
1
The term “wellbeing” is increasingly used across a wide set of academic, commercial and
2
3 public sector built environment arenas. The academic literature that investigates wellbeing in
4 the built environment can be distinguished between studies at an urban planning scale, i.e.
5 cities and local neighbourhoods, and studies at a post-occupancy building scale, i.e.
6 individual buildings across a variety of typologies. The post-occupancy literature that
7
addresses wellbeing (in a broad sense) within individual buildings is substantial, addressing
8
a variety of typologies including housing, commercial offices, industrial workplaces,
9
healthcare, care homes and elderly housing, schools, universities, academic workplaces,
10
retail and service sector, and energy efficient and low carbon buildings.
11
12
13 Whilst widely used, the term “wellbeing” is without clear definition. Typically, wellbeing is
14 considered synonymous with health, usually mental health6 7 8 9 and more rarely with
15 physical health10 11. It is also often used pragmatically, relating to comfort and indoor
16
environmental quality in the built environment. However, this generally denotes a lack of
17
18
negative problems bFeing caused by the indoor environment rather than it promoting an
improved state of comfort. Many studies define wellbeing as a combination of health and
19
o
20 comfort12 13, or health, comfort and happiness14. The inclusion of happiness suggests that
21 wellbeing refers to somethirng broader than a combination of health-related and pragmatic
22 needs being fulfilled. In relatio n, quality of life is a much used concept in studies of wellbeing
P
23
and the built environment, typically at a scale beyond individual buildings, but remains linked
24
either to health15 or the indoor enveironment16.
25
26 e
However, a great deal of academic work exists in the social sciences which seeks to define
27
r
28 wellbeing from a broader perspective, particularly in the disciplines of economics, psychology
29 and sociology. Two key definitions can be id R entified in the existing research: hedonic
30 wellbeing and eudaimonic wellbeing17 18 19 20. Hedonic wellbeing relates to happiness and
31 perceived quality of life, whereas eudaimonic we e llbeing relates to a fuller psychological
32
concept of one’s life having purpose and an individuval having the capabilities to function
33
effectively to this end. This is known as self-determination21, or flourishing22.
34 i
e
35
36 Hedonic, also often referred to as subjective, wellbeing has received considerable scholarly
w
37 attention and is defined as a combination of life satisfaction, the presence of positive affects
38 (emotions) and lack of negative feelings23. The life satisfaction component represents a
39 cognitive evaluation of various life domains (health, finances, job, leisure, relationships, etc)
40
across a relatively long time period, i.e. something that is evaluated via a thought process.
41
The other two components are usually interpreted as affective emotions within a shorter time
42
period. More recently, there has been a growing interest in the spatial differences of
43
44 subjective wellbeing, from urban, regional to national scales, and understanding the context
45 of place in wellbeing outcomes23. There has been a similar level of interest from the public
46 sector, particularly the potential of subjective wellbeing as an alternative measure of
47 development24 and in public policy evaluation25.
48
49
Taking the notion of hedonic wellbeing into consideration suggests that a wider definition of
50
wellbeing outcomes in the built environment is required that goes beyond health, comfort and
51
52 happiness. There is existing research into the impact of energy management systems on the
53 wellbeing of occupants which takes a hedonic view of wellbeing in buildings, identifying the
54 established subjective measures of Satisfaction and Affect as most relevant26. However,
55 eudaimonic wellbeing, the psychological needs required for effective functioning, is not taken
56
into account in this model and remains undefined in relation to the built environment.
57
58

1
Employing concepts of self-determination27, wellbeing is understood to consist of a
2
3 combination of thinking, feeling and functioning. It can be defined as cognitive satisfaction
4 (achieved through goal accomplishment), the presence of positive affect (and lack of
5 negative feelings), in combination with the psychological needs of competence (personal
6 ability), relatedness (social ties) and autonomy (personal control and resilience). This can be
7
represented by measures of Satisfaction, Affect, Competence, Relatedness and Autonomy.
8
The synthesis of cognition and emotion with effective function, equating to the concept of
9
flourishing22, is of particular importance in the context of growing demands to make the case
10
for increased wellbeing outcomes leading to increases in occupant performance. Health and
11
12 comfort are excluded from this conceptualisation of wellbeing in the built environment as they
13 are separate concepts and represent other, discrete outcomes produced by buildings.
14 There is a lack of systematic, academically-informed design guidelines to promote the
15
development of buildings which generate wellbeing outcomes in the end users. A range of
16
academic research exists which offers guidelines for various design features, including
17
18
studies of a specific Felement of indoor environmental quality, a particular building typology,
the impact of colour, and a small number relating to the management of buildings to promote
19
o
20 occupant wellbeing. Further, a variety of industry publications represent sources of advice on
21 wellbeing in the built envirornment, including the wealth of building certification schemes
22 globally offering a range of fra meworks and checklists for the design of green buildings
P
23
(BREEAM, LEED, Green Star), and more recently, for healthy buildings (WELL). However,
24
they rarely offer guidelines beyonde health and comfort-related elements and do not consider
25
a fuller, psychological conceptualisation of wellbeing.
26 e
27
r
28 In relation, only a small number of approaches and even fewer tools exist for the
29 measurement of wellbeing outcomes in the b R uilt environment. Several frameworks and
30 toolkits have been published in recent industry reports2 3 4 to capture the impact of the built
31 environment on wellbeing and other outcomes s e uch as health, satisfaction, and performance.
32
However, there is no direct measure of wellbeing thvat currently exists beyond self-report
33
questions. Academic work on measuring wellbeing tends to be split between the cognitive
34 i
(measuring long term satisfaction) and the affective (meeasuring short term emotions).
35
36 Research typically focuses on preventing health or comfort-related problems due to building
w
37 design, rather than considering the potential psychological benefits of positive stimuli in the
38 environment. As a result, there is a lack of evidence-based research that investigates the
39 ways that the built environment can influence wellbeing outcomes, and particularly when
40
defined in terms of individual flourishing.
41
42
As a result there are plentiful opportunities for both research and practice to drive learning
43
44 about wellbeing outcomes in buildings. Considerable further investigation is required to
45 understand the complex interrelations between wellbeing outcomes, physical building design,
46 organisational culture, and individual practices. Therefore, there is a need to promote a
47 wider, psychologically-informed definition of wellbeing in the built environment and to develop
48
a related approach for its capture and measurement. There is currently a lack of robust
49
wellbeing measures that can be applied in post-occupancy evaluations of buildings, and
50
overcoming this gap is critical for the effective transfer of new knowledge into replicable,
51
52 evidence-based design for the advancement of wellbeing in future development.
53
54
55 3.0 Wellbeing valuation in practice
56
57
58

This section introduces a novel wellbeing valuation approach consisting of a multi-item scale
2
3 to measure and quantify the wellbeing outcomes of building users in an objective and cost
4 effective manner, followed by the monetisation of the results using techniques from Social
5 Return on Investment (SROI), a social impact methodology, to produce transferable reporting
6 metrics. The approach represents the first output in the development of a toolkit that can
7
evidence the commercial case for people-centred design.
8
9
3.1 The Building Wellbeing scale
10
The first part of the wellbeing valuation approach is a multi-item scale. Its development was
11
12 based on the fuller, psychologically-informed definition of wellbeing as flourishing. As
13 outlined above it is made up of five components: Satisfaction, Affect, Competence,
14 Relatedness and Autonomy, termed the SACRA model. It was developed in reference to two
15
existing, academically developed and validated, multi-item scales for measuring wellbeing in
16
individuals or populations, i.e. not in relation to the built environment. The first scale is the
17
18
Warwick-Edinburgh FMental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS)28 and the second is the
Questionnaire for Eudaimonic Wellbeing (QEWB)29. Both scales are made up of a set of
19
o
20 Likert style items, where respondents rate their agreement on a five point scale. The
21 WEMWBS is made up of 14r positively worded items, and whereas the QEWB is made up of
22 21 items with a mixture of pos itive and negative wording. The items of the WEMWBS and
P
23
QEWB were categorised according to the SACRA components of Satisfaction, Affect,
24
Competence, Relatedness and Auetonomy, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

The scale has been piloted in a series of case building typologies, including commercial
44
offices, non-clinical healthcare centres, university libraries and student residential halls
45
during 2016 and 2017, with more than 2,000 responses collected overall. This data has been
46
47 used to validate the scale in an iterative manner using the Rasch model, a psychometric
48 approach for analysing and validating categorical data, specifically multi-item scales, as a
49 function of the trade-off between respondent traits and the item difficulty. The WEMWBS was
50 also validated using this method. The iterative approach meant that small changes could be
51
made to the scale items as required before the next pilot. Analysis has shown a good fit to
52
model expectations, as would be expected from a scale that is based on two pre-existing and
53
academically validated scales. There were some observable ceiling effects where fit was
54
skewed towards items with a higher difficulty. In practice, this meant that high numbers of
55
56 building users were able to select “Strongly agree” and achieve maximum scores of five on
57
58

the majority of the items. Therefore, additional items with increased difficulty were added to
2
3 the scale in order to provide a more accurate measure of high levels of wellbeing. For
4 example, items such as “I feel joyful when I’m in this building” are less likely to elicit top
5 scores than “I feel at ease when I’m in this building”.
6
7
In addition, the 5 point Likert scale was changed from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 to -2, -1, 0, +1, +2. This
8
was a decision to make it more intuitive to understand whether a score is signifying a positive
9
or negative finding for wellbeing. On version 1 of the scale, a score of less than 50%
10
suggests that wellbeing is low, whereas it actually means that wellbeing is negatively
11
12 impacted by the building, i.e. the building is actively reducing user wellbeing. Updated
13 versions of the scale make this clearer, as a score of less than 0% represents negative
14 wellbeing and score above 0% represents positive wellbeing.
15
16

17
18

example due to gender bias, will be removed from the scale to produce a final, validated

o
20 version. The most up-to-date version of the scale is presented in Figure 5.

50 3.2 Valuation using SROI
51
The second aspect of the wellbeing valuation approach is the monetisation of the quantitative
52
wellbeing scores produced by the Building Wellbeing scale, using impact reporting
53
techniques from Social Return on Investment (SROI). Assigning a monetary value to
54
55 wellbeing outcomes is anticipated to enhance transferability compared to typical post-
56
57
58
Page 10 of 16
59
60 http://mc.manuscriptcentral.com/bsert

Building Services Engineering Research and Technology Page 12 of 33
1
occupancy evaluation summaries, facilitating the dissemination and implementation of
2
3 findings within the design and construction industry30.
4
5 SROI is a methodology designed for the social enterprise sector to measure and account for
6 a wider concept of value for the attainment of multi-bottom lines. It was originally developed
7
in the US by the Roberts Enterprise Development Fund (REDF) in the mid-1990s. It has
8
been further developed by the New Economics Foundation (nef) in the UK since the late
9
1990s with a widely applicable stakeholder emphasis and a replicable, standardised
10
methodology. It is based on traditional cost-benefit analysis and assigns a monetary value to
11
12 social returns using financial proxies, which are compared against the level of investment to
13 produce an SROI ratio of costs to social outcomes. An SROI analysis can be retrospective or
14 prospective, encompass the value generated by an entire organisation or focus on specific
15
programmes or projects. It is one of the most developed social impact methodologies, being
16
designed to measure the outcomes of an intervention, rather than solely tracking outputs30.
17
18
Its monetisation techFnique facilitates the comparison of otherwise incommensurable benefits
across different activities. Based on real data, the results are disseminated using ‘return on
19
o
20 investment’ language that is familiar with investors and commissioners. It is widely used in
21 the UK social enterprise serctor to evidence organisational impact and is endorsed by the
22 Cabinet Office. SROI has ach ieved a significant deal of traction within the social enterprise
P
23 sector31 and, increasingly, public policy32 33 and commercial industry34.
24
e
25
The SROI methodology has six stages as set out in The Guide to Social Return on
26 e
Investment35:
27
r
28
29 1. Establishing scope and identifying ke R y stakeholders
30 2. Mapping outcomes
31 3. Evidencing outcomes and giving them a e value
32
4. Establishing impact v
33
5. Calculating the SROI
34 i
6. Reporting, using and embedding e
35
36
w
37
Watson and Whitley36 provide a detailed account of applying SROI to the built environment,
38
39 which is not an established practice. The third stage of the SROI methodology is applied to
40 the wellbeing data collected using the Building Wellbeing scale in order to place a value on
41 the quantitative wellbeing scores. The SROI methodology uses financial proxies to assign a
42
value to the outcomes under study, an alternative to traditional cost-benefit analysis methods
43
such as preference-based valuation37, A suitable financial proxy has been identified in
44
HACT’s Guide to Using the Wellbeing Valuation Approach38, which values wellbeing at
45
£36,776 per individual per year. This figure can be adjusted to make it applicable to the time
46
47 spent in the building under study, for example, a daily or weekly value would be better suited
48 to employees in an office, whereas an hourly value would be better suited to visitors of a
49 healthcare centre. The value of wellbeing to an individual is therefore £100.78 per day, or
50
£4.20 an hour. The adjusted value is multiplied by the average time spent in the building per
51
end user per year, and by the total number of end users, to produce the total value
52
generated by that building in wellbeing outcomes over a one year period. The inherent
53
subjectivity of the valuation process requires that it is made fully transparent, a core principle
54
55 of the SROI methodology35.
56
57
58

The total wellbeing value is then multiplied by the quantitative wellbeing score collected
2
3 during the user survey, which is inputted as a percentage to remove deadweight from the
4 total. It is also possible to consider attribution at this point, that is, the proportion of wellbeing
5 that can be attributed to the building as opposed to other factors like Facilities Management,
6 organisational culture, or human factors. This information can be gathered during the user
7
survey by asking end users to report how much of their wellbeing they believe is due to the
8
building design. An average is calculated and removed from the total, producing a final
9
impact-adjusted valuation for wellbeing.
10
11
12 An SROI ratio can be calculated by dividing the wellbeing figure by the building costs, i.e. the
13 design fees, contract sum and the furniture, fittings and equipment (FF&E) cost. The SROI

43
44 The rapid rise of the wellbeing agenda in the built environment suggests that user-centred
45 priorities are gaining ground alongside traditional economic and environmental imperatives in
46 the design and construction industry. The significance of wellbeing to the commercial
47 property sector is set to intensify as organisations and end users alike demand people-

approach to defining and measuring wellbeing. The importance of thorough and robust
51
52 learning loops in the design process will become evident and the need for user-centred
53 evaluation unavoidable. This represents a timely and exciting opportunity for the diffusion of
54 novel methodologies and metrics that can capture, measure and disseminate the impact of
55 the built environment to inform commissioning, tendering, high level design and briefing

1.0 Introduction

37
Wellbeing has emerged as an influential agenda in the built environment in recent years1,
38
39 promoting the social and, significantly, the economic aspects of triple bottom line
40 sustainability. It embodies an accessible and affirmative goal for occupants and practitioners
41 alike, compared to the technical discourse of restraint that surrounds energy efficiency. Its
42 growing prominence is reflected in the emergence of new valuation practices in the built
43
environment, particularly around the “business case” for wellbeing and a range of associated
44
metrics and frameworks for this end2 3 4. Interestingly, increased wellbeing is often
45
associated with anticipated improvements in occupant performance, particularly productivity2,
46
47 yet the existing frameworks for evaluation do not explicitly prove this relationship, nor
48 generate learning about how it can be achieved in practice. As the property market
49 increasingly demands user-centred environments, evidence-based design proven to deliver
50 wellbeing outcomes for end users is essential. The challenge of capturing and disseminating
51
this evidence to a range of expert and non-expert audiences is therefore a topical
52
professional concern, and requires an evaluative shift away from measuring building
53
performance towards measuring the outcomes experienced by people5.

3 The term “wellbeing” is increasingly used across a wide set of academic, commercial and
4 public sector built environment arenas. The academic literature that investigates wellbeing in
5 the built environment can be distinguished between studies at an urban planning scale, i.e.
6 cities and local neighbourhoods, and studies at a post-occupancy building scale, i.e.
7
individual buildings across a variety of typologies. The post-occupancy literature that
8
addresses wellbeing (in a broad sense) within individual buildings is substantial, addressing
9
a variety of typologies including housing, commercial offices, industrial workplaces,
10
healthcare, care homes and elderly housing, schools, universities, academic workplaces,
11
12 retail and service sector, and energy efficient and low carbon buildings.
13
14 Whilst widely used, the term “wellbeing” is without clear definition. Typically, wellbeing is
15 considered synonymous with health, usually mental health6 7 8 9 and more rarely with
16
physical health10 11. It is also often used pragmatically, relating to comfort and indoor
17
18
environmental qualitFy in the built environment. However, this generally denotes a lack of
negative problems being caused by the indoor environment rather than it promoting an
19
o
20 improved state of comfort. Many studies define wellbeing as a combination of health and
21 comfort12 13, or health, comrfort and happiness14. The inclusion of happiness suggests that
22 wellbeing refers to something broader than a combination of health-related and pragmatic
P
23
needs being fulfilled. In relation, quality of life is a much used concept in studies of wellbeing
24
and the built environment, typicallye at a scale beyond individual buildings, but remains linked
25
either to health15 or the indoor environment16.

28 However, a great deal of academic work exists in the social sciences which seeks to define
29 wellbeing from a broader perspective, particu R larly in the disciplines of economics, psychology
30 and sociology. Two key definitions can be identified in the existing research: hedonic
31 wellbeing and eudaimonic wellbeing17 18 19 20. He e donic wellbeing relates to happiness and
32
perceived quality of life, whereas eudaimonic wellbveing relates to a fuller psychological
33
concept of one’s life having purpose and an individual having the capabilities to function
34 i
effectively to this end. This is known as self-determinatioen21, or flourishing22.
35
36
w
37 Hedonic, also often referred to as subjective, wellbeing has received considerable scholarly
38 attention and is defined as a combination of life satisfaction, the presence of positive affects
39 (emotions) and lack of negative feelings23. The life satisfaction component represents a
40
cognitive evaluation of various life domains (health, finances, job, leisure, relationships, etc)
41
across a relatively long time period, i.e. something that is evaluated via a thought process.
42
The other two components are usually interpreted as affective emotions within a shorter time
43
44 period. More recently, there has been a growing interest in the spatial differences of
45 subjective wellbeing, from urban, regional to national scales, and understanding the context
46 of place in wellbeing outcomes23. There has been a similar level of interest from the public
47 sector, particularly the potential of subjective wellbeing as an alternative measure of
48 development24 and in public policy evaluation25.

50
Taking the notion of hedonic wellbeing into consideration suggests that a wider definition of
51
52 wellbeing outcomes in the built environment is required that goes beyond health, comfort and
53 happiness. There is existing research into the impact of energy management systems on the
54 wellbeing of occupants which takes a hedonic view of wellbeing in buildings, identifying the
55 established subjective measures of Satisfaction and Affect as most relevant26. However,
